newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Troubles could jolt S.Korean business to reform.
newsitem.headline: Troubles could jolt S.Korean business to reform.

text.p: A shock decision by two well known South Korean business names to sell property, affiliates and other assets to pay crushing debts could be just the jolt the country's bloated corporates need, analysts said.

"I think this is good for the economy in the long term," said Lee Jung-ja, head of research at HSBC James Capel. "Korean companies will begin to realise that they have to protect the company's net worth."
The Jinro Group, the country's largest distilled spirit maker, announced on Friday it would sell or merge at least 10 of its 24 affiliates.
Jinro, the 19th-ranked group, earlier said it would need 500 billion won ($560 million) in emergency loans. Its debts were estimated at 3.2 trillion won.

Buckling under an estimated 3.7 trillion won in debts, Ssangyong Motor Co Ltd, the fourth-largest carmaker, said it would sell its headquarters building and other assets. Ssangyong is an affiliate of the sixth-ranked Ssangyong Group.
Jinro and Ssangyong are not the only conglomerates, known as "chaebol", rumoured to be in trouble.

"I think there is a list of companies with extraordinarily high levels of gearing," said David Kadarauch, head of research at Jardine Fleming. "One would have to be very brave to bet against additional headlines of bankruptcies."
But he said he was not sure whether the asset sales of Jinro and Ssangyong Motor was the start of a trend. "It isn't going to be anything that takes the world by storm like the mini-skirt did."
Chaebols have a long history of rushing headlong into new business lines and capacity expansions even when market realities dictated otherwise.

This bigger-is-better philosopy worked fine when the South Korean economy was roaring along at a double-digit pace and the government freely directed credit to favored businesses, often bailing out those that failed.

But South Korea's coddled business community now faces a sobering new reality: The economy has slowed and the government, pushed to change by external and internal forces, has adopted an increasingly laissez-faire posture toward the chaebols.
Last month, in the aftermath of the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co and Sammi Steel Co, Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik warned that the era of government bailouts had ended.
"We must bravely liquidate companies that are operating on the margins," Kang said.
Kadarauch of Jardine Fleming said he believed the government was serious about ending bailouts and would not rescue either Jinro or Ssangyong Motor.

"I think the government will put pressure on the Ssangyong Group to do whatever it has to do to avoid Ssangyong Motor's bankruptcy, but the government will not mount a rescue. I think in this respect, the government has come a long way," Kadarauch said.
Lee of HSBC James Capel said the failure of any of Korea's banks would speed chaebol reforms.
"It's radical, but if one bank goes bankrupt, the transition period will be shortened. Maybe it will take four or five years. If the transition occurs moderately, it will take 10 years," Lee said.
